steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our robotics paper on fast reconstruction of meshes from point clouds of deforming objects, so a robot can track soft objects as they change shape. Motivate it, contrast with 3D and 4D reconstruction work, describe our approach, and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation: robots interacting with soft objects
- Seeing the object: online reconstruction from point cloud streams
- Prior 3D and 4D reconstruction work and its limits
- Our approach: deform and track a template mesh
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation
  - robot-soft object interaction: milestone not yet hit in robotics
  - e.g. robotic hand: quickly learn how unseen soft object changes shape when manipulated; continuously track deformations to adapt grasping
- Seeing the object
  - first step to dexterous manipulation of complex objects
  - model: live stream of point clouds of deforming object -> online reconstruction to trackable deforming meshes
  - point clouds from RGB-D cameras at different angles around object
- Prior work
  - meshes from point clouds: long-studied in computer graphics
  - 3D reconstruction: one mesh per point cloud; 4D reconstruction: meshes for a sequence of deforming point clouds
  - both focus on accurate refined meshes; time efficiency compromised
  - most 4D works learn canonical (template) mesh -> separate model per object category; focus on humans and animals
  - 3D: implicit algorithms with marching cubes accurate but slow; explicit models deforming template meshes fast but poor accuracy and topology
  - 3D works do not apply to time dimension -> no tracking of vertex positions; limiting for robotics
- Our approach
  - balance speed and accuracy
  - template mesh from first point cloud via SOTA implicit method, right topology, 25\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz}
  - main focus: deformed meshes for remaining frames by continuously deforming and tracking template
  - assumption: topology does not change within sequence; template has same topology as any frame
  - model (Fig. 1): encoder + decoder for encoding of deformed point cloud; Real-NVP component deforms template given encoding
  - inference 0.017 seconds, template 3000 vertices, point cloud 5000 points; Omen Desktop(24-core, 3.2GHz Intel Core i9-12900K CPU, 64GB memory, NVIDIA GeForce 3090 GPU with 24GB memory)
- Contributions (trained model)
  - online deformable meshes at 58\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} (3000-vertex template, 5000-point cloud)
  - generalizes to deformations of different object categories
  - tracks vertices

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The interaction between robots and soft objects is a milestone in robotics that has not been hit yet. For instance, a robotic hand should be able to learn quickly how an unseen soft object changes shape while it is being manipulated, and it should be able to keep tracking the deformations of the soft object so it can adapt how it grasps it.

The first step towards dexterous manipulation of complex objects is to see the object. This can be done with a model that takes a live stream of point clouds of a deforming object as input and does an online reconstruction into deforming meshes that can be tracked. The point clouds would be collected with RGB-D cameras placed at different angles around the object.

Creating meshes from point clouds has been studied for a long time in computer graphics. 3D reconstruction works generate a mesh for one point cloud, and 4D reconstruction works generate meshes for a sequence of deforming point clouds. Both kinds of works mainly focus on generating refined meshes accurately, so time efficiency is compromised. Also, most of the 4D reconstruction works are based on learning the canonical (or template) mesh, which means they have to train a separate model for each object category, and they mainly focus on humans and animals. In 3D reconstruction, implicit algorithms that use marching cubes are accurate but not time efficient, and explicit models that deform one or more initial template meshes are fast but have poor accuracy and topology. Overall, the prior 3D reconstruction works do not apply to the time dimension, so they do not allow tracking the vertex positions of the deformed meshes. This is limiting for robotics applications.

- Our approach
  - balance speed and accuracy
  - template mesh from first point cloud via SOTA implicit method, right topology, 25\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz}
  - focus: deformed meshes for remaining frames by deforming and tracking template
  - topology assumed unchanged within sequence
  - model (Fig. 1): encoder + decoder -> encoding of deformed point cloud; Real-NVP component deforms template
  - 0.017 seconds inference, 3000-vertex template, 5000-point cloud, Omen Desktop(24-core, 3.2GHz Intel Core i9-12900K CPU, 64GB memory, NVIDIA GeForce 3090 GPU with 24GB memory)
- Contributions (trained model)
  - online deformable meshes at 58\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz}
  - generalizes across object categories
  - tracks vertices

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The interaction between robots and soft objects is a milestone in robotics that has not been hit yet. For instance, a robotic hand should be able to learn quickly how an unseen soft object changes shape while it is being manipulated, and it should be able to keep tracking the deformations of the soft object so it can adapt how it grasps it.

The first step towards dexterous manipulation of complex objects is to see the object. This can be done with a model that takes a live stream of point clouds of a deforming object as input and does an online reconstruction into deforming meshes that can be tracked. The point clouds would be collected with RGB-D cameras placed at different angles around the object.

Creating meshes from point clouds has been studied for a long time in computer graphics. 3D reconstruction works generate a mesh for one point cloud, and 4D reconstruction works generate meshes for a sequence of deforming point clouds. Both kinds of works mainly focus on generating refined meshes accurately, so time efficiency is compromised. Also, most of the 4D reconstruction works are based on learning the canonical (or template) mesh, which means they have to train a separate model for each object category, and they mainly focus on humans and animals. In 3D reconstruction, implicit algorithms that use marching cubes are accurate but not time efficient, and explicit models that deform one or more initial template meshes are fast but have poor accuracy and topology. Overall, the prior 3D reconstruction works do not apply to the time dimension, so they do not allow tracking the vertex positions of the deformed meshes. This is limiting for robotics applications.

In our work we want a balance between speed and accuracy, so we assume that a template mesh can be generated from the first point cloud of the deforming point cloud sequence with a SOTA method, e.g. an existing one which works in the implicit domain and generates meshes with the right topology at a speed of 25\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz}. Our work mainly focuses on generating deformed meshes for the rest of the deformed point cloud frames by continuously deforming and tracking the template mesh. We assume that within a sequence of deforming point clouds of an object the topology does not change, so the template mesh has the same topology as the deformed point cloud of any frame in the sequence. To predict the mesh coordinates of the deformed mesh we use our model, shown in Fig. 1, which has an encoder and decoder that extract an encoding from the deformed point cloud and a Real-NVP component that deforms the template mesh given the deformed encoding. The pipeline has an inference speed of 0.017 seconds for a template mesh of 3000 vertices and a point cloud of 5000 points on an Omen Desktop(24-core, 3.2GHz Intel Core i9-12900K CPU, 64GB memory, NVIDIA GeForce 3090 GPU with 24GB memory).

In summary, our main contributions are a trained model that:

- Can generate deformable meshes online at 58\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} given a template mesh of 3000 vertices and a deformed point cloud of 5000 points.

- Generalizes to the deformations of different object categories.

- Can track the vertices.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The interaction between robots and soft objects is a milestone yet to be reached in the field of robotics. For instance, a robotic hand should be able to quickly learn how an unseen soft object changes shape while it is manipulated, and should be able to continuously track the deformations of a soft object to adapt its grasping method accordingly.

The first step towards dexterous manipulation of complex objects is seeing the object. This can be achieved through a model that takes a live stream of point clouds of a deforming object as input and performs an online reconstruction to trackable deforming meshes. The stream of point clouds would be collected via RGB-D cameras positioned at different angles around the object.

Creating meshes from point clouds is a long-studied problem in the computer graphics field. Works in 3D reconstruction generate a mesh for one point cloud [1,2,3,4], while 4D reconstruction works generate meshes for a sequence of deforming point clouds [5,6,7,8,9]. Both focus mainly on the accurate generation of refined meshes, and hence time efficiency is compromised. Furthermore, most 4D reconstruction works are based on learning the canonical (or template) mesh, which limits them to training a separate model for each object category, with the main focus on humans and animals. In 3D reconstruction, on one hand, implicit algorithms [1] which use marching cubes are accurate but time inefficient; on the other hand, explicit models [2,3,4] that deform one or more initial template meshes are fast but have poor accuracy and topology. Overall, prior works in 3D reconstruction do not apply to the time dimension and hence do not allow for tracking the vertex positions of the deformed meshes, which is limiting in robotics applications.

In our work, to find a balance between speed and accuracy, we assume a template mesh can be generated from the first point cloud of the deforming point cloud sequence using a SOTA method, e.g. [1] which operates in the implicit domain and generates meshes of the right topology with a speed of 25\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz}. Our work focuses mainly on generating deformed meshes for the remaining deformed point cloud frames by continuously deforming and tracking the template mesh. We assume that within a sequence of deforming point clouds of an object, the topology does not change, and hence the template mesh has the same topology as the deformed point cloud of any frame within the sequence. To predict the mesh coordinates of the deformed mesh, we use our model, illustrated in Fig. 1, which consists of an encoder and decoder for extracting an encoding from the deformed point cloud and a Real-NVP [10] component which deforms the template mesh given the deformed encoding. The resulting pipeline has an inference speed of 0.017 seconds for a template mesh of 3000 vertices and a point cloud of 5000 points on an Omen Desktop(24-core, 3.2GHz Intel Core i9-12900K CPU, 64GB memory, NVIDIA GeForce 3090 GPU with 24GB memory).

In summary, our main contributions are a trained model:

- With the capacity to generate deformable meshes in an online manner at 58\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} given a template mesh of 3000 vertices and a deformed point cloud of 5000 points.

- Generalizable to the deformations of different object categories.

- With the capacity to track the vertices.
